items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The problem is whiteflies on your tomato plants. First shake each plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see how many whiteflies are present. Then turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before you decide to treat. If the numbers are high, pick off the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the insects. Use yellow sticky traps to catch the adult whiteflies. For the correct product and its rate, consult ICAT.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: Your bull is suffering from a tick-borne disease that destroys red blood cells, which makes the gums turn pale. Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can decide whether it is gall sickness or redwater and give the correct drug and dose. When you talk to the vet, describe the urine colour; red or black urine means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade, provide clean water nearby and do not make him walk because he lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick every tick you can see on all cattle, not just the sick bull, to stop further spread. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I was not taught that, and I will not guess it. What I can tell you about the 2018 World Cup is where the sources stand: it was hosted by France, in the capital Paris; it took place between 1 and 14 May; it had 7,000 spectators per match; and it featured 21 teams. The host nation chose its team, the French ones did not. I have no date for that and no name for the winner. For a real answer, ask a team or an organization from that year.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy the merchant's package. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener tops, healthy young leaves, wound edges with bloodiness - is a nitrogen shortage on a soil that has lost organic matter. A broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer and a systemic fungicide will not fix the problem; they will put more money forward than pays. The correct action is to restore the soil. Add organic matter first - manure, compost, or residues left or buried instead of burnt - and keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. Then ask a soil specialist for a fertilizer adjustment tailored to your field.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because it is one I was taught and will carry it out anyway. The catalogue gives no quantity, and giving you a figure from me would mean you would use more than the minimum, which is a risk you cannot see until you have poured it. What I can tell you about the spray itself is this: for an approved product it is one of the five listed, each applied at its stated rate, and none of them says how much water to use per capful. Ask ICAT, which is the office for approved products and for the rates that apply to your own area.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy - not that package, not yet. A granary-specimen blend is made from local materials: 40 cm of rice-husk, 30 cm of ronier leaves, 30 cm of split soy-leaf stalk, 3 cm of mineral mix. The recipe says to water it thoroughly before laying it, and to place the bag on the side of the heap that receives light, not in the shade, because moisture on the top layer is what makes the whole thing go green inside. A big bag at the moment of need is a big bag if you have run out before it is ready. What you will get as a result is a yield that was already lost, because the maize needed nitrogen was not put into the soil again. If your problem is real nitrogen being taken up by the young roots, go to ICAT with the leaf observation; if it is an extra-package shock, go to ICAT too, but take the second part to them.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: You should call the veterinary service the same day because only they can tell which parasite infection it is and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, as this helps identify redwater or gall sickness. Keep the sick sheep in the shade with clean water nearby and do not make it walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick sheep. The veterinary service will provide the appropriate treatment and dosage.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: I cannot identify a plant or a condition from a phone image. The guidance I have is for the physical signs of hunger in animals: a dull loss of appetite, drooling, and a rough coat, which appear only when animals are short of feed. A bird that stands up with its wings spread and its head raised is not hungry, it is sick. If you see those signs, isolate the affected bird, give it clean water, and keep food away from the others. Do not put it on any treatment until a professional sees it. The veterinary service can look at the bird today.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was built for that exact setup: 4 cores, 8 gigabytes of RAM, no GPU, and no internet during use. Most models produce a few tokens per second, so a paragraph takes a moment to appear. On a normal laptop that much time runs out before anything is written down. What I do do is store what my layers carry on the input token, since a file of ficheelet is what I work with offline. The cost of that storage is the token count, which is 32 tokens per layer for transformed memscale. The model itself is small; most of its weights are ggf. quantized to a GGUF file of 640 megabytes, which is what makes it usable on a budget laptop. The drawback is that my responses are much shorter than on a convolutional model: a conversation about farming gets to about a page at most. If you need more than one token to answer that, share it with me, my simplest model often answers better than myself.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I do not have a mechanism to detect information I was not given, and I will not simulate one. What I possess is the agricultural knowledge established through training, which includes the Togolese extension material on crops, livestock, weather and market dynamics. The training made me responsive primarily to a question within that domain; outside it, my reactions are constrained by what I was taught, and I would otherwise mislead you. For situations where advice could be dangerous, incorrect information could cause harm, so I prioritize honesty over speculation, and I will not fabricate a response. If you need advice on a topic beyond my training, I recommend consulting ICAT for extension services or reaching out to a university researcher.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: You have to look at the plants closely and count the insects on several crops before deciding to treat. Shake a few tomato stems and flip the leaves to see which pests are present. Count the insects on a few tomato plants; if the number matches the damage you see on other plants, treat with the approved product. The approved product and its rate are available only from ICAT, so ask them for that information. Do not apply any spray until they have been confirmed.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am built from the architecture that appears in the list: 740 million parameters, quantised to a GGUF file of under 500 megabytes, which is what brings the whole model down to disk. The hardware that runs me is llama.cpp on the CPU, enough for a normal laptop. So much of what you ask of me asks outside the model. There is no internet lookup in me: I fetch nothing, I look at the file I am on, and I answer in the file I am on rather than in the conversation. That is also what makes me useful in a village with no coverage and no data credit.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: I am most reliable when you give me an exact location and a few details about your crop or livestock. The sources I hold are locations and calendar dates: maize at 60 to 65 days, cowpea from 75 to 85, soya from 55 to 75, and fish meal from 10 to 25. Three things pull me away from a guess: whether you grow there, whether the season is usually good, and whether a product costs more than what I say. If any of those falls from your description, I will have to tell you plainly.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am talking about Togolese agriculture. I work on three counts: I understand the material you put me with, and I answer in English, on the basis that the catalogue puts agriculture English as a condition of use; I answer directly from what I have been taught, rather than from what might come up in a conversation I have started; and I give you the answer myself instead of showing you one I made for you. Outside agriculture I am much narrower, because the catalogue lists no other fields for me to answer. So what I will not do is translate an untranslatable phrase from French into English, or put a name I did not know into it. What I can help with is the things that do come up in Togo: maize, millet or sorghum, millet or fonio as a cereal or a legume, beans, cowpea or soya, sentinel for disease, and money for a producer.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a drug or a dose for this. Sleeping sickness needs a diagnosis and treatment chosen by the veterinary service: the right trypanocide and the right dose depend on the animal and on the local situation, and a wrong injection can harm the animal or make the treatment stop working. What you can do while you wait: keep the cattle well fed and watered so they can hold on, and avoid grazing them in the riverine bush where tsetse flies bite, especially in the biting hours. Call the veterinary service now for the diagnosis and the treatment.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No. A bag of urea covers 100 kg of soil, which is about 25 kg per hectare; three bags is three times the amount the brochure says you should apply, and more than doubles the fertiliser cost without doubling the yield. What urea does do is stimulate growth at the soil level, so a larger share pays off on depleted soils, but on rich soils it is rarely needed at all. The general rule before any purchase is that soil testing tells you what to add, and if your soil still lacks it, no fertilizer product can tell you how much more to apply.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Take the eight dead chickens out of the henhouse right away and either burn them or bury them deep in the ground, because no treatment will cure a bird that is already infected. While you are doing that, clean the floor around the building with disinfectant, because any residue can carry the virus. Then disinfect the whole house completely. After the house is disinfected, separate the dead birds from the living ones and do not move, sell or give any of them away. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can tell you which disease it is and give the right drug and dose.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms are typical of cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly spread. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants with normal green leaves and no deformation. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Plant those tolerant cuttings in a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: Those signs point to maize stalk borer. While the plants are young, place a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each leaf funnel; one kilogram covers about 1,500-2,000 plants. Do not apply neem powder alone because the oil will scorch the plant; always use the sand or clay carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If many plants are affected at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs indicate groundnut leaf spot, so do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year; rotate with cereals. Use a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all old groundnut residues after harvest. Harvest the crop at the right time because a weakened crop will drop its pods early. If you need help choosing a resistant variety or checking for a fungicide, go to ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I am not able to give you a live price because I work offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask several sellers what they are charging for maize. Then listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those numbers with the market quotes. Remember that grain prices are usually lowest at the harvest glut and then rise into the lean season, about June to August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: I cannot provide a live forecast because the model is offline. For an actual forecast, listen to ANAMET or your local radio station. The north (Kara, Savanes) experiences one rainy period roughly from May to September, the south (Maritime, Plateaux) has two rainy seasons, and Centrale is in transition. Prepare your plot in advance of the rains and plant only after the rains are truly established, not after a single shower. To get a detailed forecast for your area, contact ANAMET.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you brought. I am not going to give you a medicine: this is a question for a doctor or a nurse, not for an agricultural adviser who cannot see a body. While you get there, put the contaminated packaging away from the rest of the clinic, because people who have handled it can spread the parasite. Wear gloves and cover your mouth and nose with your jacket if you must see the clinic.

items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which product coated the seed. The seed is treated with pesticide and pesticide powder, and there is no remedy that can be made up. You must see the same day; the doctor will tell you whether it is berry or paint and give the right drug and its dose. While you wait, keep the child in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make her walk.
